source_text:
Iam enim nenio ad illa auspicia et auguria Romana, quae summo : labore collecta testatus es et paenitenter omissa. et obseruata feliciter.
Clodius scilicet et Flaminius et unus ideo exercitus perdiderunt, quod pullorum solistimum tripudium exspectandum non putauerunt. quid Regulus?
nonne auguria seruauit et captus est? Mancinus religionem tenuit, et sub iugum missus est et deditus. pullos edaces habuit et Paulus, apud Cannas tamen cum maiore populi Romani parte prostratus est.
Gaius Caesar, ne ante brumam in Africam nauigia transmitteret, auguriis et auspiciis renitentibus, spreuit: eo acus et nauigauit et uicit.
quae uero et quanta de oraculis prosequar? post mortem Amphiaraus uentura respondit, qui proditum iri se ob monile ab uxore nesciuit. Tiresias caecus futura uidebat, qui praesentia non uidebat.
de Pyrro Ennius Apollinis Pythi responsa confinxit, cum iam Apollo uersus facere desisset: cuius tunc cautum illud et ambiguum defecit oraculum, cum et politiores homines et minus creduli esse coeperunt. et Demosthenes, quod sciret responsa simulata, φιλιππίζειν Pythiam querebatur.
At nonnumquam tamen ueritatem uel auspicia uel oracula tetigerunt. quamquam inter multa mendacia uideri possit industriam casus imitatus, adgrediar tamen fontem ipsum erroris et prauitatis, unde omnis caligo ista manauit, et altius eruere aperire manifestius. spiritus sunt insinceri, uagi, a caelesti uigore terrenis labibus et cupiditatibus degrauati.
isti igitur spiritus, posteaquam simplicitatem substantiae suae onusti et inmersi uitiis perdiderunt, ad solacium calamitatis suae non desinunt perditi iam perdere et deprauati errorem prauitatis infundere et alienati a Deo inductis prauis religionibus a Deo segregare.
eos spiritus daemonas esse poetae sciunt, philosophi disserunt, Socrates nouit, qui ad nutum et arbitrium adsidentis sibi daemonis uel declinabat negotia uel petebat.
magi quoque non tantum sciunt daemonas, sed etiam quicquid miraculi ludunt, per daemonas faciunt: illis adspirantibus et infundentibus praestigias edunt, uel quae non sunt uideri, uel quae sunt non uideri.
eorum magorum et eloquio et negotio primus Hostanes et uerum Deum merita maiestate prosequitur et angelos, id est ministros et nuntios Dei sed ueri, eius uenerationi nouit adsistere, ut et nutu ipso et uultu domini territi contremescant. idem etiam daemonas prodidit terrenos, uagos, humanitatis inimicos.
quid Plato, qui inuenire Deum negotium credidit, nonne et angelos sine negotio narrat et daemonas? et in Symposio etiam suo naturam daemonum exprimere conititur? uult enim esse substantiam inter mortalem inmortalemque, id est inter corpus et spiritum mediam, terreni ponderis et caelestis leuitatis admixtione concretam, ex qua monet etiam t nos procupidinem amoris, et dicit informari et inlabi pectoribus. humanis et sensum mouere et adfectus fingere et ardorem cupiditatis infundere.
thought_title: Roman auspices, oracles, and the demons behind them
orientation: Octavius is answering Caecilius's defense of Roman religion by showing that augury and oracles have failed, and that whatever truth they sometimes touch comes from demons.
pass_a_gloss: Now indeed I come to those auspices and auguries of Rome, which with the greatest labor collected you have testified to and with regret omitted and observed successfully. Clodius of course and Flaminius and one army lost for this reason, that they did not think the most favorable tripudium of the chickens had to be awaited. What about Regulus? Did he not observe the auguries and was captured? Mancinus held to religion, and was sent under the yoke and handed over. Paulus also had greedy chickens, yet at Cannae he was laid low with the greater part of the Roman people. Gaius Caesar, although the auguries and auspices resisted, so that he should not send ships across to Africa before the winter solstice, scorned them: the more easily he both sailed and conquered. What indeed and how much shall I pursue about oracles? After death Amphiaraus answered things to come, who did not know that he was going to be betrayed by his wife for a necklace. Tiresias the blind man saw future things, who did not see present things. About Pyrrhus Ennius invented responses of Pythian Apollo, although Apollo had already ceased to make verses: whose cautious and ambiguous oracle then failed, when men began to be both more refined and less credulous. And Demosthenes, because he knew the responses were faked, complained that the Pythia was playing Philip's side. But sometimes nevertheless either auspices or oracles touched the truth. Although among many lies chance imitating diligence can seem possible, I will nevertheless approach the very source of error and depravity, from which all this darkness has flowed, and dig it out more deeply and reveal it more clearly. They are unclean spirits, wandering, weighed down from heavenly vigor by earthly stains and desires. These spirits therefore, after they lost the simplicity of their substance, loaded and immersed in vices, for the solace of their calamity do not cease, already ruined, to ruin and, depraved, to pour in the error of depravity and, alienated from God, to separate from God by introducing depraved religions. That these spirits are demons the poets know, the philosophers discuss, Socrates knew, who at the nod and judgment of the demon sitting by him either declined affairs or sought them. The magi also not only know demons, but also whatever miracle they perform, they do through demons: with those inspiring and pouring in, they produce illusions, either things that are not to seem to be, or things that are to seem not to be. Of those magi both in speech and in work the first Hostanes both attends to the true God with deserved majesty and knows that angels, that is ministers and messengers of the true God, stand by for his worship, so that terrified by the very nod and face of the Lord they tremble. The same man also revealed demons as earthly, wandering, enemies of humanity. What about Plato, who believed finding God was a task, does he not also without task tell of angels and demons? And in his Symposium too does he not try to express the nature of demons? For he wants there to be a substance between mortal and immortal, that is between body and spirit, a middle thing, concreted by the mixture of earthly weight and heavenly lightness, from which he also warns that the desire of love is formed in us, and he says it is shaped and slips into human breasts and moves the senses and fashions feelings and pours in the heat of desire.

choices.english: the most favorable tripudium of the chickens
choices.why: Keeps the technical augural term tripudium and renders solistimum as superlative of favorable omen, preserving the ritual sense.
Uses the glossary term religion for religio and keeps the verb's force of adherence.
Renders insinceri as unclean and uagi as wandering, matching the demon description used later in the work.
Uses the glossary term religion for religionibus and keeps prauis as depraved to match prauitatis.

choices.english: that the Pythia was playing Philip's side
choices.why: Keeps the Greek verb's political sense of favoring Philip, as Demosthenes' accusation.
rejected: that the Pythia was bribed by Philip

choices.term: terreni ponderis et caelestis leuitatis admixtione concretam
choices.english: concreted by the mixture of earthly weight and heavenly lightness
choices.why: Literal rendering of the physical terms Plato uses for the demonic substance.
rejected: compounded of earthly heaviness and heavenly lightness
made solid by mixing earthly weight and heavenly lightness

pass_b_english: Now I come to those Roman auspices and auguries which you said were gathered with enormous effort, regretfully abandoned, and happily observed. Clodius, Flaminius, and one army lost for this reason: they did not think they should wait for the most favorable sacred-chicken omen. What about Regulus? Did he not keep the auguries, and was captured? Mancinus held to religion, and he was sent under the yoke and handed over. Paulus had greedy chickens, and at Cannae he was laid low along with the greater part of the Roman people. Gaius Caesar scorned auguries and auspices that resisted his sending ships to Africa before the winter solstice; thus he both sailed and conquered.

What should I say about oracles, and how much? After his death Amphiaraus answered what was to come, though he did not know he would be betrayed by his wife for a necklace. Tiresias, blind, saw the future, though he could not see the present. Ennius invented the responses of Pythian Apollo for Pyrrhus, since Apollo had by then stopped making verses; that cautious and ambiguous oracle failed when people became more refined and less credulous. Demosthenes too, because he knew the responses were faked, complained that the Pythia was speaking for Philip.

But sometimes, however, auspices or oracles have touched the truth. Although among many lies it may seem that chance imitated diligence, I will still approach the very source of error and depravity, from which all this darkness has flowed, and dig it out more deeply and reveal it more clearly. They are deceitful spirits, wandering, weighed down from heavenly vigor by earthly stains and desires. These spirits, then, burdened and immersed in vices, having lost the simplicity of their substance, though already ruined, do not cease to ruin others, as comfort for their calamity; already depraved, they pour in the error of their depravity and, alienated from God, they separate people from God by introducing depraved religions.

The poets know that these spirits are demons; the philosophers discuss them; Socrates knew them, who at the nod and judgment of the demon attending him would either decline undertakings or seek them. The magi too not only know demons, but whatever miracle they perform, they do it through demons: with those spirits inspiring and pouring in, they produce illusions, either making things that are not appear to be, or making things that are appear not to be. Hostanes, first among those magi in both eloquence and practice, honors the true God with the majesty He deserves, and knows that angels, that is, ministers and messengers of the true God, stand in attendance on His worship, so that at the very nod and face of the Lord they tremble with terror. He also exposed demons as earthly, wandering, enemies of humanity.

What about Plato, who thought finding God was a task? Does he not easily speak of angels and demons too? And in his Symposium does he not try to express the nature of demons? He wants there to be a substance midway between mortal and immortal, that is, between body and spirit, compounded by the mixture of earthly weight and heavenly lightness. From this, he warns, comes even for us the desire of love; and says it is formed and slips into human hearts, moves the senses, fashions emotions, and pours in the ardor of desire.
notes: The source text contains 'eo acus et nauigauit et uicit', where 'acus' appears to be a corruption or variant; the gloss renders it as 'the more easily' based on the likely intended 'eo facilius'.

problems.why: glossary: banned rendering 'unclean spirits' (use 'demons')
lint glossary: banned rendering of daemones; use 'demons' ('unclean spirits')

edits.old: They are unclean spirits, wandering, weighed down from heavenly vigor by earthly stains and desires.
edits.new: They are demons, wandering, weighed down from heavenly vigor by earthly stains and desires.

fixed: Changed 'unclean spirits' to 'demons' because the source term is 'spiritus sunt insinceri' and the glossary bans 'unclean spirits' for daemones; the English should use 'demons'.

problems.why: Latin 'unus' means 'one' (army), not 'Junius'; no such name appears.
problems.fix: Clodius, Flaminius, and one army lost for this reason
problems.ruling: Latin 'et unus' = 'and one', no name Junius; translation adds false name

problems.why: 'solistimum' means 'most favorable/fortunate', but 'tripudium' is specifically the sacred chicken's feeding as omen, not just 'tripudium'.
problems.fix: the most favorable feeding of the sacred chickens
problems.ruling: no ruling

problems.quote: he sailed all the more easily
problems.source_quote: eo facilius et nauigauit et uicit
problems.why: 'eo' = 'therefore/thus', not 'all the more easily'; 'facilius' modifies both sailing and conquering.
problems.fix: thus he both sailed and conquered more easily
problems.ruling: no ruling

problems.why: 'φιλιππίζειν' means 'to speak for Philip/Philipize', not 'playing Philip's side'; Demosthenes accused Pythia of being Philip's mouthpiece.
problems.fix: complained that the Pythia was speaking for Philip
problems.ruling: no ruling

problems.why: English skips 'insinceri' (deceitful/impure) and makes them demons immediately; Latin says 'spirits' first, identifies as demons later.
problems.fix: They are deceitful spirits, wandering
problems.ruling: Latin calls them 'spiritus' then 'daemonas'; English jumps to 'they are demons' skipping 'insinceri'

problems.why: Misplaced modifier: Latin says they lost simplicity because they were burdened/drowned; English says they lost simplicity first, then were burdened.
problems.fix: after, burdened and immersed in vices, they lost the simplicity of their substance
problems.ruling: no ruling

problems.why: 'sine negotio' means 'easily, without difficulty', not 'without any task'; ironic contrast with Plato finding God difficult.
problems.fix: Does he not easily speak of angels and demons too?
problems.ruling: no ruling

problems.why: 'concreted' is archaic/technical; 'concretam' means 'compounded, formed together, solidified'.
problems.fix: compounded by the mixture
problems.ruling: no ruling

problems.quote: From this, he says, comes the desire of love
problems.source_quote: ex qua monet etiam nos procupidinem amoris
problems.why: Omits 'etiam nos' (us too/also us); 'procupidinem' is 'excessive desire', not just 'desire'.
problems.fix: From this, he warns, comes even for us the excessive desire of love
problems.ruling: no ruling

problems.quote: it is shaped and slips into human hearts
problems.source_quote: et dicit informari et inlabi pectoribus humanis
problems.why: Subject confusion: 'it' refers to the substance/demon nature, but Plato says love itself is formed and slips in; 'informari' = 'to be formed/shaped' (middle voice).
problems.fix: and says it is formed and slips into human hearts
problems.ruling: no ruling

problems.why: Latin has 'paenitenter omissa. et obseruata feliciter' (regretfully abandoned, and happily observed); English merges awkwardly, losing the ironic contrast.
problems.fix: regretfully abandoned—and happily observed
problems.ruling: no ruling

problems.source_quote: At nonnumquam tamen ueritatem uel auspicia uel oracula tetigerunt
problems.why: No 'you say' in Latin; this is Octavius's own concessive statement, not addressing an interlocutor directly.
problems.fix: But sometimes, however, auspices or oracles have touched the truth
problems.ruling: Latin lacks 'you say'; English inserts it, altering speaker

problems.quote: making things that are not appear not to be
problems.why: Should be 'making things that are appear not to be'; double negative error in English.
problems.fix: or making things that are appear not to be
problems.ruling: Latin 'uel quae sunt non uideri' = 'or those which are not to be seen'; English double negative misstates

problems.quote: and knows that angels—that is, ministers and messengers of God, but the true God
problems.source_quote: angelos, id est ministros et nuntios Dei sed ueri
problems.why: Misplaced 'sed ueri': modifies 'Dei' (of the true God), not 'ministros et nuntios'; 'but the true God' is ungrammatical and misleading.
problems.fix: angels—that is, ministers and messengers of the true God
problems.ruling: Latin 'angelos, id est ministros et nuntios Dei sed ueri' = 'angels, i.e., ministers and messengers of the true God'; English misplaces 'sed ueri'

problems.quote: at the very nod and face of their Lord
problems.why: 'domini' = of the Lord/God (the true God just mentioned), not 'their Lord'; Hostanes speaks of God's angels trembling before God.
problems.fix: at the very nod and face of the Lord
problems.ruling: no ruling

solistimum tripudium is a technical augural term for the sacred chickens' favorable eating; changed to 'sacred-chicken omen'.

onusti et inmersi uitiis modifies the spirits, not a temporal sequence; changed 'after, burdened... they lost' to 'burdened... having lost'.

problems.quote: Paulus had greedy chickens too, yet at Cannae he was laid low along with the greater part of the Roman people.
problems.source_quote: pullos edaces habuit et Paulus, apud Cannas tamen cum maiore populi Romani parte prostratus est.
problems.why: The greedy chickens (pullos edaces) belong to Mancinus in the Latin, not to Paulus.
problems.fix: Mancinus had greedy chickens, and Paulus, at Cannae, was laid low together with the greater part of the Roman people.

problems.why: The punctuation and 'already lost—from destroying others' is garbled; 'perditi iam perdere' = 'though already ruined, [they] still ruin [others]'.
problems.fix: though already ruined, they do not cease to ruin others, as comfort for their calamity
problems.ruling: English garbles ‘non desinunt perditi iam perdere…’, losing ‘though already ruined they still ruin others’.

last_rejected.quote: does he not easily speak of angels and demons too
last_rejected.source_quote: nonne et angelos sine negotio narrat et daemonas
last_rejected.why: 'sine negotio' means 'without difficulty/unhesitatingly', not 'easily' in sense of casually; more importantly 'narrat' is 'relates/tells of', not 'speak of'.

last_rejected.quote: He wants there to be a substance midway between mortal and immortal—that is, between body and spirit

last_rejected.fix: He wants there to be a substance midway between mortal and immortal—that is, a substance midway between body and spirit
last_rejected.ruling: 'mediam' agrees with 'substantiam', giving a substance midway; translation mirrors this, not an error.

polish.changed: Clarified sentence structure and pronoun references, smoothed awkward phrasing, and made the speaker's argument flow naturally for modern readers while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.quote: blind fortune or uncertain nature rules
notes.why: These terms shift between Caecilius's skeptical 'fortune/nature' and Octavius's theological 'fate' without clear distinction of who uses which.
notes.fix: Clarify that 'fate' is God's ordering, 'fortune' is blind chance.

notes.quote: Socrates knew them, who at the nod and judgment of the demon attending him would either decline undertakings or seek them
notes.why: 'demon' here is Greek daimonion (divine sign), not Christian demon; confusing given earlier demonology.
notes.fix: 'divine sign' or note the different sense.

notes.quote: Socrates knew them, who at the nod and judgment of the demon attending him
notes.why: Not Scripture but presented as authoritative; Plato's Apology 31c-d, not biblical.
Hostanes is an obscure Persian magus cited without identification.
notes.fix: Gloss: Hostanes, a Persian magus or priest.

notes.quote: Ennius invented the responses of Pythian Apollo for Pyrrhus
notes.why: Ennius, Pyrrhus, and the Pythia are cited without identification.
notes.fix: Gloss: Ennius, Roman poet; Pyrrhus, Greek king; Pythia, Delphic priestess.

notes.quote: Demosthenes too, because he knew the responses were faked, complained that the Pythia was speaking for Philip
notes.why: Demosthenes and Philip are cited without identification.
notes.fix: Gloss: Demosthenes, Athenian orator; Philip, king of Macedon.

notes.quote: Amphiaraus answered what was to come, though he did not know he would be betrayed by his wife for a necklace
notes.why: Amphiaraus and the mythic backstory are unexplained.
notes.fix: Gloss: Amphiaraus, a seer in Greek myth, betrayed by his wife Eriphyle.

notes.quote: Tiresias, blind, saw the future, though he could not see the present
notes.fix: Gloss: Tiresias, the blind prophet of Greek myth.
